pairs.rationale: Both letters address people in the dispersion. James names the twelve tribes and calls himself a servant; Peter names chosen resident aliens and particular regions. These different addresses are compared without identifying every recipient.

James calls for joy amid varied trials; Romans speaks of boasting in afflictions because affliction produces perseverance. The shared response is grounded in the stated endurance/perseverance-producing process, with the different circumstances preserved.

James says the testing of faith produces endurance. Romans connects affliction, perseverance and proven character in its own sequence; the comparison does not silently exchange testing and proven character.

James seeks endurance completing its work so the readers lack nothing. Romans continues from perseverance to proven character and hope. Both give endurance a further constructive outcome, while describing that outcome differently.

James directs those lacking wisdom to ask the generous God. Jesus teaches asking and receiving and contrasts human gifts with the Father giving good things. Wisdom is James’s particular requested gift, not the Gospel’s only category.
Both passages connect believing prayer with the refusal to doubt. James adds the wind-driven wave image; Matthew uses the mountain and fig tree. Neither image is substituted into the other passage.

The doubting requester is told not to expect receipt from the Lord; later James says some requests fail because they aim at pleasures. These are distinct stated obstacles to receiving, not interchangeable accusations against every petitioner.

The description of divided mind recurs when James calls those of divided mind to purify their hearts. The later command supplies a concrete corrective to the instability described here without identifying the same individual.

James permits the lowly brother to boast in exaltation; Mary’s song describes the lifting up of the lowly. The comparison concerns the reversal of low status, not an identification of the brother with a person in the song.

James compares the passing rich person with a grass flower. Peter’s scriptural grass-and-flower comparison applies to all flesh and its glory. The broader target image supports the source comparison without restricting Peter to wealthy people.

Both describe grass drying and its flower falling. James applies the image to the rich person’s pursuits; Peter contrasts mortal transience with the enduring word, so the two applications remain distinct.

Both speak of a divine promise to those who love Him. Here the approved endurance receives the crown of life; later the poor chosen rich in faith inherit the kingdom. The different reward descriptions are preserved.

James denies that God is tempted by evil or tempts anyone. Paul describes God’s faithfulness in limiting temptation and providing an escape for endurance. The target concerns God’s help within temptation, not God enticing people to evil.

James locates enticement in a person’s own desire. Jesus lists evil things coming from within the human heart and defiling a person. The common inward source does not make every desire identical with each listed offense.

James traces desire conceiving sin and matured sin bringing death. Romans names death as sin’s wages and contrasts God’s gift of life. The target supports the stated sin–death outcome without reproducing James’s birth sequence.

The warning not to be led astray follows the denial that God tempts and the explanation of desire, sin and death. This retained passage states the particular account against which the warning must be read.

James identifies the Father of lights as the source of good and complete giving. Jesus says the heavenly Father gives good things to those asking. James’s denial of variation adds a claim not stated in the target.

James says He gave us birth through the word of truth by His will; Peter describes being born anew through God’s living, enduring word. The shared word-mediated birth is compared without replacing James’s firstfruits image.

The command to be slow to speak corresponds to the later account of not stumbling in speech and bridling the body. Hearing and anger remain additional commands in the source, rather than claims supplied by the target.

James denies that human anger accomplishes God’s righteousness. Ephesians commands anger without sin, a limit on its duration and no opportunity for the devil. These are related restraints, not identical statements that all anger is already sinful.

pairs.relationship: putting away evil and receiving nourishment
pairs.rationale: Both begin by putting away named evils and then direct readers to receive sustaining instruction or nourishment. James calls the implanted word able to save souls; Peter uses the image of newborn infants desiring milk.

James contrasts doing the word with self-deceiving hearing alone. Jesus contrasts hearers who do His words with hearers who do not, using houses with different foundations. The target supplies an explicit enactment of the same hearing–doing distinction.

pairs.relationship: the hearer who does not do
pairs.rationale: James’s mirror example begins with hearing without doing. Luke likewise contrasts hearing and doing with hearing without doing, after the challenge about calling Jesus Lord while not doing what He says. The illustrations remain different.

The mirror viewer goes away and forgets; Luke’s hearer fails to act and the house falls. The comparison is the ineffective result of an unacted-on encounter, not a claim that Luke contains a mirror or forgetfulness.

James joins continuing in the law of freedom with doing and blessing. Jesus joins remaining in His word with discipleship, knowing truth and freedom. The target does not rename every occurrence of law as the Gospel saying.

James calls unbridled speech incompatible with worthwhile religion. Later he exposes the same mouth blessing the Lord and cursing people as conduct that ought not occur. The concrete contradiction illustrates the source’s warning about the tongue.

pairs.relationship: purity and care for the vulnerable
pairs.rationale: James combines undefiled religion with care for orphans and widows and freedom from worldly stain. Isaiah combines washing away evil with seeking justice for orphan and widow. The shared ethical pattern includes both cleansing and protection.

James prohibits acts of favoritism within faith in the Lord Jesus Christ. Romans states that there is no partiality with God. The target provides the divine impartiality relevant to the source’s command, not a description of its gathering.

pairs.relationship: wealth and access to a gathering
pairs.rationale: James contrasts a splendidly dressed rich entrant with a poorly clothed entrant. Jesus contrasts inviting rich neighbors with inviting the poor and disabled. Both expose the treatment of people at gatherings according to material advantage, with different situations.

James describes honored seating for the splendidly dressed and humiliating directions to the poor. Leviticus forbids partiality to poor or powerful in judgment. The source’s seating example is a particular discriminatory practice, not Leviticus’s identical setting.

James calls the discriminators judges with evil thoughts. Leviticus commands righteous judgment without partiality to poor or powerful. This directly compares the condemned kind of judgment with the prescribed impartial judgment.

James speaks of God choosing the poor to be rich in faith and heirs of the promised kingdom. Jesus pronounces the poor blessed because the kingdom of God is theirs. James’s added faith and love language is retained as its own formulation.

The accusation that the rich oppress and drag people into courts is complemented by James’s later charges of withheld wages, condemnation and murder. The later passage supplies concrete abuses without identifying every wealthy person with one named defendant.

James accuses the rich oppressors of blaspheming the good name called over the readers. Romans describes God’s name blasphemed among nations because of others’ conduct. Both connect a divine name with dishonoring behavior, but assign the roles differently.

James quotes the command to love one’s neighbor as oneself as the royal law. Leviticus supplies that command in its own context of rejecting vengeance and resentment. The quotation does not turn favoritism into acceptable neighbor-love.

James says favoritism is sin exposed by the law. Leviticus expressly prohibits partiality and requires righteous judgment. The retained prohibition provides concrete legal content rather than a merely general reference to wrongdoing.

pairs.relationship: the obligation to the whole law
pairs.rationale: James reasons that stumbling at one point makes the keeper accountable for all. Galatians cites the requirement to continue in all things written in the law. Their particular arguments differ, while both reject selective treatment of its obligations.

Both passages expressly list the prohibitions of adultery and murder. James uses their common speaker to explain transgression despite selective obedience; Romans gathers commandments under neighbor-love. The shared commands support comparison without merging those arguments.

The command to speak and act as persons judged through a law of freedom recalls the earlier law of freedom whose continuing doer is blessed. The two passages connect this law with conduct rather than bare hearing.

James warns of judgment without mercy for the person who showed none. Jesus links receiving forgiveness with forgiving others. Mercy and forgiveness are compared as treatment of others bearing on one’s own judgment, without treating the terms as identical.

James questions whether a claimed faith lacking works can save. Jesus distinguishes saying Lord from doing the Father’s will when speaking of entering the kingdom. Both challenge an unaccompanied profession, without erasing their different formulations.

pairs.relationship: a fellow believer in material need
pairs.rationale: James names a brother or sister lacking clothing and daily food. John describes seeing a brother in need while possessing material resources. The target makes explicit the obligation presented by such a concrete need, not a different spiritualized lack.

James rejects a warm farewell without supplying bodily necessities. John rejects closing compassion to a needy brother and calls for love in deed and truth rather than speech alone. Both expose words failing to meet material need.

James calls faith without works dead by itself. Galatians describes faith working through love. The target offers an explicitly active description of faith, while the differing circumcision setting and James’s dead-faith judgment are not silently equated.

pairs.relationship: visible evidence of an inward claim
pairs.rationale: James challenges the display of faith apart from works and offers to show it by works. Jesus uses fruit to recognize trees and false prophets. The comparison concerns evidence in conduct, not an assertion that the target uses James’s faith terminology.

James’s affirmation that God is one recalls the confession concerning the Lord in Deuteronomy. James adds that even demons believe and shudder; that added warning is not represented as part of Deuteronomy’s words.

pairs.relationship: faith and the place of works
pairs.rationale: James calls faith apart from works idle. Ephesians distinguishes salvation as God’s gift through faith from boasting in works, then describes creation in Christ for good works. The comparison preserves this ordering rather than claiming both sentences say the same thing.

James refers to Abraham offering Isaac on the altar. Genesis narrates the altar, the binding and Abraham’s action before the divine interruption. James’s justification language is its interpretation, not wording inserted into Genesis.

James says Abraham’s faith worked with his works and was completed through them. Hebrews explicitly describes offering Isaac by faith and Abraham’s reasoning about resurrection. These are distinct interpretations of the same offering, with neither reduced to the other.

James repeats Abraham’s believing God and its reckoning as righteousness. Genesis names him Abram and contains that statement in the promise narrative. James’s additional friend-of-God title is not falsely included in the retained Genesis verse.

pairs.relationship: different formulations of faith and works
pairs.rationale: James denies justification by faith alone and speaks of works; Romans speaks of justification by faith apart from works of law. The comparison preserves both formulations and their different qualifications rather than silently removing alone or of law.

James cites Rahab welcoming the messengers and sending them by another way. Joshua narrates her lowering them through the window and directing them to the hill country to avoid the pursuers. James’s justified-by-works judgment is not inserted into that narrative.

James concludes with the body-and-spirit analogy to restate faith without works as dead. The earlier assertion already calls workless faith dead by itself. The analogy explains the same conclusion without requiring an external account of the soul.

James warns prospective teachers of greater judgment. Jesus distinguishes servants according to knowledge and responsibility and says more is required of those given more. The target supports differentiated accountability without claiming its servants are specifically teachers.

James links not stumbling in speech with bridling the whole body. The earlier warning calls religion futile when a person does not bridle the tongue. The repeated restraint image connects speech with the integrity of the person’s conduct.

The bit guiding a horse’s whole body is followed by a small rudder guiding a large ship and the small tongue boasting greatly. These retained analogies explain the scale contrast; they do not claim the body is literally a horse.

The large ship’s small rudder corresponds to the bit guiding a horse’s whole body. These paired control analogies explain disproportionate influence before the application to the tongue; neither is merely an unrelated reference to travel.

The small member and forest-fire image lead into the tongue explicitly called a fire staining the whole body. The retained explanation identifies the moral application of the image rather than treating every occurrence of fire as a cross-reference.

James describes the tongue staining the whole body. Jesus says what comes from the mouth comes from the heart and defiles a person, then names offenses. The target supports the defiling speech connection without supplying James’s Gehenna and wheel-of-life images.

James lists animal kinds that humankind tames. Genesis describes humans in God’s image and their rule over fish, birds and land creatures. The source’s taming claim differs from the target’s commission to rule and should not be quoted as identical.

James calls the tongue restless evil full of deadly poison. Romans’s description of corrupt speech includes poison under lips. Both use poison for destructive human speech, without turning either description into a literal biological claim.

James condemns cursing humans made in God’s likeness while blessing the Lord and Father. Genesis states the divine image and likeness in the creation of humankind. The creation statement supplies the reason the source gives for rejecting that contradiction.

pairs.relationship: what should come from the mouth
pairs.rationale: James says blessing and cursing from one mouth ought not happen. Ephesians forbids corrupt speech and directs speech useful for building up and giving grace. Both judge speech by its effect, with the source’s particular blessing–cursing contradiction preserved.

The question about sweet and bitter water from one spring illustrates the preceding contradiction of blessing the Lord and cursing people from the same mouth. The retained application supplies the specific speech problem behind the spring image.

James denies that a fig tree produces olives or a vine figs. Jesus likewise argues from trees and their fruit to the recognition of conduct. The specific fruit examples differ, while the source–product consistency is explicit in both.

James asks the wise person to show works in good conduct and wisdom’s gentleness. Paul directs spiritual people to restore a transgressor in a spirit of gentleness. The shared gentleness is enacted in conduct, while the target gives one particular restorative task.

James rejects bitter jealousy and selfish ambition as grounds for boasting against truth. Galatians includes jealousy and selfish ambitions among works of the flesh. The target’s broader list is not attributed to every reader James addresses.

James labels the corrupt wisdom earthly, merely natural and demonic rather than from above. Paul says the natural person does not receive the things of God’s Spirit. This compares resistance to divine wisdom without assigning all three James labels to Paul’s phrase.

James associates jealousy and selfish ambition with disorder and foul practice. Paul contrasts disorder with peace in describing God and the churches. The disorder–peace contrast is concrete, while the respective disputes remain different.

James describes heavenly wisdom as pure, peaceable, considerate, open to persuasion and fruitful in mercy. Galatians lists the Spirit’s fruit, including peace, kindness and gentleness. The related moral qualities support comparison without treating the two lists or their wording as interchangeable.

James joins peacemaking, peace-sown fruit and righteousness. Jesus blesses peacemakers and names them sons of God. Both commend peacemaking, while the source’s sowing image and the target’s filial promise remain distinct.

James locates conflicts among the readers in pleasures waging war in their members. Peter describes fleshly desires waging war against the soul. Both portray desire as an active combatant, with different stated arenas and outcomes.

James first describes desire, conflict and failure to ask; the next verse describes asking wrongly for pleasures. The retained continuation distinguishes absent asking from wrongly aimed asking rather than accusing every unanswered petitioner of murder.

James says requests aimed at spending on pleasures fail. John links confidence in being heard with asking according to His will. The passages state different criteria for prayer; the target is not a promise that every desired pleasure must be granted.

James calls friendship with the world hostility toward God. John prohibits love for the world and says its desires are not from the Father. The related opposition preserves friendship, love and hostility as the passages’ different expressions.

pairs.relationship: the cited saying within its argument
pairs.rationale: The question about Scripture and jealous yearning for the spirit is followed by the qualification that He gives greater grace and by the proud–humble contrast. This retained contextual response preserves lower-case spirit and does not assign an unprinted Old Testament quotation source.

James quotes God opposing the proud and giving grace to the humble. The retained Proverbs saying supplies this opposition and grace contrast. It is not replaced with an English wording or verse location from a different textual tradition.

James commands submission to God and resistance to the devil, with the devil’s flight. Peter commands vigilance and resistance firm in faith. The shared resistance is explicit, while James’s promised flight and Peter’s roaring-lion image remain separate.

James calls readers to draw near to God with a promised divine drawing near. Zechariah calls for return to the Lord and promises His return to them. The reciprocal response is compared without removing James’s cleansing and divided-mind commands.

James commands mournful repentance in place of laughter and joy in this rebuke. Jesus blesses those who mourn with promised comfort. These different speech acts connect mourning and divine response without making every form of laughter sinful.

James promises that the Lord will exalt those who humble themselves before Him. Jesus states that the self-exalting will be humbled and the self-humbling exalted. The shared reversal is explicit and does not specify a timetable.

James rejects speaking against or judging a brother and setting oneself above the law. Romans asks who the reader is to judge another’s household slave. Both challenge assuming an authority over a fellow believer that belongs elsewhere.

pairs.relationship: God able to save and destroy
pairs.rationale: James identifies one Lawgiver and Judge able to save and destroy. Jesus directs fear toward the one able to destroy soul and body in Gehenna. The target supports divine authority over destruction without supplying James’s separate lawgiver title.

James presents confident plans to travel, trade and profit. Jesus’s rich man makes confident storage and enjoyment plans before his life is demanded. Both expose future economic plans that omit life’s dependence; the target does not narrate James’s proposed journey.

James calls life a briefly appearing vapor. The Psalm describes the transience of human life and its futile activity. The retained native Greek-based Psalm location supports mortal brevity without assuming its image is word-for-word identical.

James says plans for life and action should be conditioned on the Lord’s will. Paul conditions a future return on God’s willing. The target gives a particular travel plan expressed in the manner James commends.

James calls boasting in pretensions evil. Paul says the readers’ boasting is not good in a particular case of tolerated wrongdoing. Both explicitly reject a boast, while their distinct occasions prevent treating either as a ban on every use of boasting.

James calls it sin to know the good and fail to do it. Jesus describes a slave who knows his master’s will but does not prepare or act accordingly and receives punishment. Both make known but neglected duty morally consequential.

James orders the rich to weep over coming miseries. Jesus pronounces woes upon the rich and those now laughing, including future mourning. The warnings compare present comfort and its reversal without identifying each rich hearer as one named individual.

James names rotted riches and moth-eaten garments. Jesus warns against earthly treasures destroyed by moth and consumption and contrasts heavenly treasure. Both expose the vulnerability of stored wealth, though James speaks in accusation and Jesus in instruction.

James accuses readers of storing treasure in the last days while corroded wealth testifies against them. Romans describes storing wrath for the day of wrath. The comparison concerns accumulation becoming judgment, not a claim that Romans names corroded metals.

James says withheld harvest wages cry out and the laborers’ cries reach the Lord. Deuteronomy forbids withholding a poor worker’s pay lest the worker cry to the Lord and sin be charged. The concrete wage grievance grounds the link.

James pictures indulgent people fattening their hearts on a day of slaughter. Jeremiah asks the Lord to purify the wicked for their day of slaughter. The shared judgment-day expression is compared without importing the sheep-and-gathering wording absent from this Saints Jeremiah verse.

The charge of condemning and murdering the righteous one culminates the accusations against the rich. James earlier names the rich as oppressors dragging people into courts. This connection does not identify the unnamed righteous one with a particular historical person.

James’s farmer waits for the crop and the early and late rain. Deuteronomy speaks of God giving early and latter rain for the land’s produce. The shared agricultural dependence illustrates patient waiting without making the target a direct prediction of the coming.

James commands patient, strengthened hearts because the Lord’s coming has drawn near. Paul prays that hearts be established in holiness at the Lord Jesus’s coming. The shared heart-strengthening and coming connect different exhortatory and prayer forms.

James forbids groaning against one another to avoid judgment and depicts the Judge at the doors. Jesus warns against judging with a corresponding measure of judgment. These related warnings retain James’s particular complaint and imminent-Judge image.

James calls the prophets who spoke in the Lord’s name examples of suffering and patience. Jesus recalls persecution of the prophets when addressing persecuted disciples. The target supports the remembered prophetic suffering without claiming all suffered in the same way.

James explicitly names Job’s endurance and the Lord’s outcome. Job’s conclusion recounts restoration and the Lord’s blessing of his latter things. The narrative supports the outcome allusion without inserting James’s endurance wording into Job’s closing verses.

pairs.relationship: oaths and truthful yes or no
pairs.rationale: Both prohibit swearing by heaven or earth and direct truthful yes and no. James frames the consequence as avoiding judgment; Matthew adds other oath objects and says what exceeds these is from evil. Those differences remain visible.

James directs the cheerful to sing praise while directing the sufferer to pray. Ephesians describes psalms, hymns, songs and thanksgiving to the Lord. The target supports the praise branch, not a claim that every song implies an absence of suffering.

James directs summoning Church elders to pray and anoint the sick in the Lord’s name. Mark recounts anointing many sick people with oil and healing them. The shared practice does not make Mark’s messengers identical with James’s elders.

pairs.relationship: forgiveness and restoration of the sick
pairs.rationale: James speaks of faithful prayer saving the weary sick person, the Lord raising him and conditional forgiveness of sins. Mark narrates forgiveness and the paralytic’s bodily rising at Jesus’s word. This comparison does not make sin the stated cause of every sickness.

James commands mutual confession and prayer for healing. The Psalm describes acknowledging sin to the Lord and forgiveness. The confession–forgiveness connection is retained while the Psalm’s address to God is not rewritten as mutual confession between people.

James explicitly gives three years and six months without rain after Elijah’s prayer. Jesus likewise names Elijah’s days and heaven shut for three years and six months. Luke’s statement supports the duration without supplying every detail of the prayer.

James says Elijah prayed again and heaven gave rain. Kings narrates Elijah bowing, repeated reports from his servant, a cloud and abundant rain. The narrative supports the rain’s return without inventing a printed verbatim prayer.

James considers someone led astray from truth and another turning him back. Galatians directs restoring a person caught in a transgression with gentleness and self-watchfulness. The common restorative act does not erase the differing descriptions of the offense.

James associates turning back a sinner with saving his soul from death and covering many sins. Peter says love covers a multitude of sins. The shared covering phrase is retained without deciding an unprinted identity for the possessive his or equating every context.
